blocks.title: Πώς δουλεύει η ελληνική βρισιά
blocks.text:
Greek swearing is not a list of bad words; it is a small, very productive **system** built on five or six roots, which combine with a handful of grammatical frames. Learn the roots, learn the frames, and you will understand ninety per cent of what you hear on a football terrace, in a taxi or in a sitcom.

**The roots.** (1) **μαλάκας** and its family (*μαλακία, μαλακίζομαι, μαλακισμένος*), from *μαλακός* 'soft'; literally about masturbation, but in practice about stupidity, uselessness and, between friends, simply 'mate'. (2) **γαμώ / γαμάω** 'to fuck', the most productive verb in the language: *γαμώτο, γαμάτος, άντε γαμήσου, γάμα το, γαμήθηκα, δε γαμιέται*. (3) **σκατά / χέζω** 'shit / to shit': *χέστηκα, χέσ' το, σκατόψυχος*. (4) **κώλος** 'arse', mainly as the prefix **κωλο-** 'crappy, damned'. (5) **αρχίδια / παπάρια** 'balls': nonsense, indifference, and (in *αρχιδάτος*) courage. (6) **πουτάνα**, **κερατάς**, **διάολος** and the **sacred names** (Χριστός, Παναγία, Θεός), which Greek swearing attacks more freely than most European languages.

**The frames.** Almost everything strong is built from a few slots: **γαμώ + το/την/τους + X + μου/σου** (*γαμώ το κέρατό μου, γαμώ την τύχη μου, γαμώ το σόι σου*); **στο / στ' + X + μου** 'I don't give a damn' (*στ' αρχίδια μου, στον κώλο μου*); **άντε + imperative** (*άντε γαμήσου, άντε στο διάολο*); **να + πάρει + subject** for wishes and minced oaths (*να πάρει ο διάολος, να πάρει η ευχή*); and the prefix **κωλο-** for 'bloody'.

**Intonation decides.** The same word *μαλάκα* can be a warm greeting, an exasperated sigh, a filler, or a fighting word. Read the stress, the length, the volume, what comes before (*ρε*, *έλα ρε*, *τι λες ρε*) and, above all, the relationship. A useful rule of thumb: **a swear word inside a joke, a complaint about the world or a story is light; the same word aimed at a person with a pause and eye contact is heavy.**

This lesson gives each item a strength from **0** (neutral) to **5** (taboo, never with strangers). Strength is the force of the word when *aimed at someone*; used as an exclamation about a situation (*γαμώτο! σκατά!*) everything drops by one or two points.

blocks.title: Μαλάκας: η λέξη με τις χίλιες σημασίες
blocks.text:
**ο μαλάκας** (gen. *του μαλάκα*, voc. **μαλάκα**, pl. *οι μαλάκες*) is described even by Greeks as *the* Greek word. Literally 'one who masturbates' (from *μαλακός* 'soft', older sense 'effeminate, weak'), it is used for: (a) an idiot or jerk, (b) a man who lets himself be exploited (*με πέρασε για μαλάκα* 'he took me for a fool'), and (c) **between friends, mainly young men but increasingly everyone**, a term of address like 'mate, dude, bro': *Τι λέει, μαλάκα;*

**The female forms.** *μαλάκας* is grammatically masculine, but in the vocative young women use **μαλάκα** to each other and to men just as freely. For an insult at a woman, the traditional form is **μαλακισμένη** (strength 4, only an insult, never friendly); the newer **η μαλάκω** exists but is jokey and rarer.

**ρε μαλάκα as filler.** In fast casual speech *ρε μαλάκα* (often reduced to something like *ρε μαλά'* with the last vowel swallowed) works like *like* or *dude* in American English: *Ήταν, ρε μαλάκα, τόσο ωραία!* No one is being insulted; it marks emotion and intimacy. Among friends *μαλάκα* can appear three times in a sentence.

**The family.** **η μαλακία** (pl. *μαλακίες*) is the most useful word of the group: 'nonsense, rubbish; a stupid mistake'. *Λες μαλακίες* 'you're talking bullshit'; *Έκανα μαλακία* 'I screwed up'; *Μαλακία μου* 'my bad, my mistake'; *Άσε τις μαλακίες* 'cut the crap'; *Τι μαλακία!* 'what crap / what a stupid thing'. Literal 'masturbation' sense exists but is less common than the figurative. **μαλακίζομαι** (deponent; aor. *μαλακίστηκα*) 'to act stupid, mess about, dither': *Μη μαλακίζεσαι!* 'stop messing about / don't be an idiot'. **μαλακισμένος -η -ο** 'wanker, prat' (insult only, 4). **παλιομαλάκας** 'damned idiot' (παλιο- intensifies, 4).

blocks.text:
**Rule for the learner: μαλάκα is earned, not borrowed**

Use *μαλάκα* to a Greek only after they have used it to you, in the same relaxed tone, and never as your first swear word with someone new. From a foreigner, *μαλάκα* said too early sounds either comic (best case) or as the real insult (worst case). Safe substitutes until then: **ρε φίλε** (hey man), **ρε συ** (hey you, informal), **ρε βλάκα** (playful, 1), **χαζέ / χαζή** (silly, 1).

blocks.title: Γαμώ: το πιο παραγωγικό ρήμα
blocks.text:
**γαμώ / γαμάω** (aor. *γάμησα*, passive *γαμιέμαι*, aor. pass. *γαμήθηκα*, past part. *γαμημένος*) means literally 'to fuck' and is the source of a huge family. Origin: ancient *γαμέω* 'to marry' (cf. *γάμος* 'wedding'), so do not confuse the swear verb with the wedding vocabulary: *παντρεύομαι* is 'to marry' today.

**γαμώτο!** (< *γαμώ το*, 'I fuck it') is the everyday 'damn it!'. Said to the situation, it is **2**: people say it in front of parents, colleagues, on chat shows; grandmothers may frown. It also exists as a neuter noun in *έχω γαμώτο* 'to have self-respect, pride, guts' (*Δεν έχει γαμώτο, δεν κάνει τίποτα* 'he has no drive'), colloquial-vulgar. Reinforced: **ρε γαμώτο**, **γαμώτο μου**.

**γαμάτος, -η, -ο** 'fucking great, awesome': *Γαμάτη ταινία!* Strength 3 in form, but the meaning is positive, so among young people it is everyday (2-3). Neuter **γαμάτο!** as an exclamation: 'awesome!'. Remember: **-ημένος = bad, -άτος = great.** *Γαμημένο αμάξι* 'fucking car (useless)' vs *γαμάτο αμάξι* 'awesome car'.

**γαμιέμαι**: *άντε γαμήσου!* 'fuck off! go fuck yourself!' (4); *γαμήθηκα* 'I'm fucked / I got screwed' (*Γαμήθηκα στη δουλειά σήμερα* 'I worked my arse off / it was hell today'); impersonal **δε γαμιέται** 'oh, never mind, sod it, who cares' (3); **γαμιέται ο Δίας** 'all hell is breaking loose / it's a total mess' (3, joke-mythological). **γάμα το / γάμα τα** 'forget it, fuck it, drop it' (3): *Γάμα τα, πάμε για μπίρα.*

**ο γαμιάς** 'stud, a man who sleeps around and boasts of it' (3-4; can be admiring among men). **Του γάμησα τη μάνα / του γάμησες τη μάνα** (said of a thing or task) has two opposite readings: 'you totally wrecked it' or 'you totally nailed it' (*Του γάμησες τη μάνα του τεστ!* 'you smashed that test'); 4 because *μάνα* is in it. Do not confuse with the curse **γαμώ τη μάνα σου** below.

**The frame γαμώ το X μου** curses your own luck: **γαμώ το κέρατό μου** 'fuck my life' (lit. 'I fuck my horn'; 3-4, extended jokingly to *γαμώ το κέρατό μου μέσα*); **γαμώ την τύχη μου** 'fuck my luck' (3); **γαμώ το φελέκι μου** 'damn my fate' (3, older, Turkish *felek* 'fate'). Turned outward to **σου**, the frame becomes a direct attack: **γαμώ το κέρατό σου** (4), **γαμώ το σόι σου** 'fuck your whole family' (5), **γαμώ τους πεθαμένους σου** 'fuck your dead' (5, one of the gravest insults: the dead and the mother are sacred).

blocks.title: Η μάνα: the red line
blocks.text:
Attacks on the **mother** are the heaviest part of the system because the mother is the most protected figure in Greek family culture. The full formula is **γαμώ τη μάνα σου** (5), but in practice you mostly hear the clipped **τη μάνα σου!** (also 5: the verb is understood), sometimes just **(ρε) τη μάνα σου...** muttered. Variants: **της μάνας σου το...** + a vulgar noun (5, avoid), *γαμώ τη μάνα που σε γέννησε* (5).

Two important exceptions where *μάνα* is not an attack: (1) a self-directed oath **γαμώ τη μάνα μου** is rare and sounds unhinged; (2) **του γάμησες τη μάνα** about a task or object (see above) means wrecked/nailed it. And the very common **Μάνα μου!** 'Mother!' is just a mild exclamation of shock (0-1), like *Θεέ μου*.

A mother insult between strangers is exactly the line after which many fights become physical. Between close male friends in a football or gaming context it can be thrown around as banter, but this is the riskiest banter in the language; as a foreigner, never initiate it.

blocks.title: Πώς λειτουργεί το κωλο-
items: **κωλο-** attaches to almost any noun: *κωλοκαιρός* (lousy weather), *κωλοδουλειά*, *κωλολεωφορείο*. It is the colloquial equivalent of 'bloody' or 'damn'.
Stress usually moves to the compound pattern: *καιρός → κωλοκαιρός*, *δουλειά → κωλοδουλειά*, *σπίτι → κωλόσπιτο*; with neuter -ι nouns the stress often jumps to the antepenult.

It is the same family as **παλιο-** (*παλιομαλάκας, παλιόκαιρος*) and **σκατο-** (*σκατόκαιρος*): παλιο- is milder (2), κωλο- middle (2-3), σκατο- coarser (3-4). The prefix system is treated in detail in the morphology unit.
Do not confuse **κωλύω** (learned, 'to hinder', cf. *κώλυμα* 'obstacle') with *κώλος*. Different spelling, different word: *Το κώλυμα* is an impediment, not a rude joke.
Adjective *κωλόφαρδος* 'lucky' comes from the image of a wide arse sitting on luck; no Greek hears it as very rude in a card game.

blocks.title: Αρχίδια και παπάρια
blocks.text:
**τα αρχίδια** (sing. *το αρχίδι*, almost always plural) 'balls, testicles' is the heavier word; **τα παπάρια** is the softer synonym (one grade milder, often used on TV comedies and by people who want to sound rude without being crude).

Uses: (1) **nonsense**: *Αρχίδια!* / *Παπάρια!* 'Bollocks!' 'Like hell!'; *Λέει αρχίδια* 'he's talking bollocks'; *παπάρια μάντολες* 'total rubbish' (jokey). (2) **indifference**: **στ' αρχίδια μου** 'I don't give a fuck' (*Στ' αρχίδια μου τι λέει!*), softer **στα παπάρια μου**. (3) **nothing at all**: **δεν ξέρω τ' αρχίδια μου** 'I don't know jack shit'; *δεν σκίζω και τα αρχίδια μου* 'I'm not exactly thrilled' (lit. 'I'm not tearing my balls'), a lukewarm reaction. (4) **courage**: **αρχιδάτος** 'ballsy, gutsy, a real man' (positive!), *δεν έχει αρχίδια* 'he has no balls'. (5) **a failure**: *Τα έκανε αρχίδια* 'he screwed it up' (3).

**Pronunciation:** *αρχίδια* is **ar-HÍ-dja**: the ι before α becomes a glide /j/, so it is three syllables, not four: /arˈçiðʝa/. The χ before ι is the soft palatal [ç] (like German *ich*). Foreigners who say *ar-khee-DEE-a* sound comic; Greeks find it charming but it marks you as a beginner. Likewise *παπάρια* = /paˈparʝa/, three syllables, and *σκατά* is stressed on the last syllable, not *σκάτα*.

blocks.text:
**Why only for recognition**

These words are fully part of real speech, and you will hear them in films, on the street and in lyrics, so you need to understand them. But they carry sexual content that changes the temperature of a conversation in a way *γαμώτο* or *μαλακία* does not. The sex and nightlife vocabulary itself is covered in the nightlife unit; here, just know the force and do not produce them until you are completely sure of the company.

blocks.title: Τα ιερά: from Παναγία μου to βλαστήμια
blocks.text:
Greek uses sacred names in two completely different ways, and the difference matters more than almost anything else in this lesson.

**Invocations (mild, 0-1).** *Θεέ μου! Χριστέ μου! Παναγία μου! Χριστός και Παναγία! Θεέ και Κύριε!* are exclamations of shock or despair, used by everyone, including the devout. *Παναγία μου!* is very typical of older women; *Χριστέ μου* covers surprise, fear and exasperation. *Δόξα τω Θεώ* 'thank God' and *ο Θεός να βάλει το χέρι του* 'God help us' are neutral. *Μου βγήκε η Παναγία* 'I was worn out, it was a nightmare' (lit. 'the Virgin came out of me') is colloquial, 2.

**Βλαστήμια (blasphemy, 5).** The verb **βλαστημώ** 'to blaspheme, swear' and the noun **η βλαστήμια** refer specifically to cursing the sacred: **γαμώ το Χριστό σου**, **γαμώ την Παναγία σου**, **γαμώ το Θεό σου**, *γαμώ το σταυρό σου*, *γαμώ τα καντήλια σου* (the icon oil lamps), *τον Χριστό σου μέσα*, often clipped to **το Χριστό σου!** / **την Παναγία σου!**. Note the grammar: it is *your* Christ, *your* Virgin: the speaker attacks the listener's sacred things. Plain *γαμώ το Χριστό!* without *σου* exists as an outburst at a situation and is slightly less aimed, but still 5 for most listeners.

**Why it is so strong and so common.** Greece is a country where most people are baptised Orthodox and the Church is woven into family life, so blasphemy carries real transgressive charge; at the same time it is commonplace in some working-class, rural, island and male milieus, in the army and on building sites, where a string of *καντήλια* can be just punctuation. Blasphemy was a criminal offence (Penal Code art. 198-199) until the new code of 2019 abolished it; it remains a social offence. Many Greeks who swear constantly with *μαλάκα* and *γαμώτο* will never blaspheme, and some will walk away if you do.

**Rule:** invocations yes, βλαστήμια never. Understand it, recognise it, do not produce it.

blocks.title: Γενιές, φύλο και ο ξένος που βρίζει
blocks.text:
**Generations.** People over 65 tend to use the religious and devil-based mild oaths (*να πάρει ο διάολος, Παναγία μου, ανάθεμα*) plus old-style curses; the γαμώ and μαλάκα layers exploded with post-1980s youth culture and are now the default informal register of anyone under 50. Many grandparents swear heartily, but in older styles: blasphemy from a village grandfather is not unusual, while *μαλάκα* from a grandchild may still earn a slap on the wrist.

**Gender.** Traditional norms said women should not swear, and men still often moderate their language 'in front of ladies', especially older men. In practice young urban women use *μαλάκα* to friends constantly and *γαμώτο* is gender-neutral. Sexual insults against women (*πουτάνα, καριόλα, μουνί*) are judged far more harshly when aimed at a woman than their male equivalents; a man who uses them at a woman is seen as crossing a line.

**Regions and milieus.** Islanders, Cretans and northern Greeks have reputations for colourful blasphemy; the army is a famous school of swearing; football terraces have their own chants that are pure 5. Swearing density is a marker of solidarity: in many groups not swearing at all sounds stiff.

**The foreigner who swears.** Greeks are usually **delighted** when a foreigner produces a well-timed *γαμώτο* or *μαλακίες*: it signals effort and intimacy, and gets a laugh. Most tourists know *μαλάκα* and say it wrongly, so a correctly placed *ρε μαλάκα* among friends is a badge of integration. But the line is thinner for you than for a native: a foreigner who uses 4s and 5s with strangers loses the benefit of the doubt, and an accent makes a 3 sound like a 4. Mispronounced swearing (*mala-KA*, *ar-khee-DEE-a*) sounds funny, not tough. Strategy: **listen first, mirror the level of the group, stay one step below it.**

blocks.title: Προφορά και επιτονισμός
blocks.text:
**Stress.** *μαλάκας* /maˈlakas/ stress on the middle: ma-LA-kas; vocative *μαλάκα* ma-LA-ka (never *MA-la-ka* or *ma-la-KA*). *γαμώτο* ga-MO-to; *γαμάτο* ga-MA-to; *σκατά* ska-TA; *κερατάς* ke-ra-TAS, vocative *κερατά* ke-ra-TA; *διάολε* DJA-o-le (ια = /ja/ glide). *παπάρια* pa-PA-rja, *αρχίδια* ar-HI-dja.

**Elisions.** Swearing is fast speech: *στ' αρχίδια μου* (στα → στ'), *χέσ' το* (χέσε το), *γάμα τα*, *τα 'κανα σκατά* (έκανα → 'κανα), *άι στο διάολο* (άντε → άι), *ρε μαλά'* (final vowel swallowed). In writing people use the apostrophe: *Γάμα τα κι άσ' τα*.

**Assimilation and consonants.** *γ* before *α, ο* is a voiced fricative [ɣ], not a [g]: *γαμώτο* is [ɣaˈmoto]. The *ντ* in *άντε* is [nd] or just [d]. *χ* before *ε, ι* is palatal [ç]: *χέστηκα* [ˈçestika]. *ψωλή* [psoˈli] vs *ψωμί* [psoˈmi]: listen and keep them apart.

**Intonation.** Affectionate *μαλάκα* is usually short, light and comes at the start or end of a phrase with a smile in the voice (*Έλα, μαλάκα!* rising); the insult is heavier, with lengthened first syllable and falling pitch (*Μααλάκα...*), or shouted. *Γαμώτο* to oneself is clipped and falling. *Άντε γαμήσου* laughing has a lilting, sing-song melody; said in anger it is flat and separated: *Άντε. Γαμήσου.* Emphasis on the *σου* in *τη μάνα ΣΟΥ* makes it targeted.

**Gesture tip.** Many swear words come with a flick of the hand, the chin, or the *μούντζα* (see the insults lesson): learn to read the hand as well as the words.

**Common mistakes / false friends**

- **γαμάω ≠ to marry.** Ancient *γαμέω* did mean 'marry', and *γάμος* is still 'wedding', but the modern verb is purely sexual. *Θα παντρευτούμε* 'we'll get married'; *Πότε είναι ο γάμος;* 'when is the wedding?' is perfectly innocent.
- **γαμημένος (bad) ≠ γαμάτος (great).** Swapping them reverses your meaning.
- **μαλακός ≠ μαλάκας.** *μαλακός* 'soft' is a normal adjective (*μαλακό μαξιλάρι*); *η μαλάκω* is a jokey feminine of *μαλάκας*, not 'soft'.
- **ψωλή / ψωμί, πούτσα / πούλμαν** etc.: keep vowels and consonants precise.
- **σκατά is plural** in form: *τα σκατά*, so *τα έκανα σκατά* not *το έκανα σκατό*.
- **κερατάς to a man you don't know** is not affectionate; the friendly *ρε κερατά* needs the smile and the relationship.
- **Don't translate English 'fucking' with γαμημένος everywhere.** Greek intensifies more often with *πολύ, τρομερά, θεο- (θεόκλειστος), κωλο-* or with rhythm and *ρε*, than with an adjective inserted mid-phrase.
- **Βλαστήμια ≠ βρισιά.** *βρισιά / βρίζω* is swearing and insulting in general; *βλαστήμια / βλαστημώ* is cursing the sacred (though in loose speech *βλαστημάει* can mean 'he swears a lot').

blocks.title: Διάλογος 1: Δύο κολλητοί μετά το ματς

items.el: Α: Ρε μαλάκα, είδες το δεύτερο γκολ; Γαμάτο!
items.en: A: Dude, did you see the second goal? Fucking awesome!

items.el: Β: Ναι, αλλά στο τέλος τα κάναμε σκατά, γαμώτο.
items.en: B: Yeah, but at the end we screwed it all up, damn it.

items.el: Α: Ο διαιτητής, ρε! Τι μαλακία ήταν αυτό το πέναλτι;
items.en: A: The ref, man! What kind of bullshit was that penalty?

items.el: Β: Άσ' τον, ρε, χέστηκα για τον διαιτητή. Ο τερματοφύλακας φταίει.
items.en: B: Forget him, I couldn't give a shit about the ref. The goalkeeper's to blame.

items.el: Α: Αυτός; Κωλοφαρδία είχε όλη τη σεζόν, τώρα του τελείωσε.
items.en: A: Him? He's had dumb luck the whole season, now it's run out.

items.el: Β: Γαμώ την τύχη μου, πάλι εκατό ευρώ έχασα στο στοίχημα.
items.en: B: Just my fucking luck, I lost a hundred euros on the bet again.

items.el: Α: Μαλάκα μου... Σου είπα να μην παίζεις.
items.en: A: Oh man... I told you not to bet.

items.el: Β: Άντε γαμήσου! (γελώντας)
items.en: B: Fuck off! (laughing)

items.el: Α: Χαχα, καλά, γάμα τα. Πάμε για μπίρα;
items.en: A: Haha, OK, forget it. Shall we go for a beer?

items.el: Β: Πάμε. Αλλά κερνάς εσύ, κερατά, εσύ κέρδισες.
items.en: B: Let's go. But you're buying, you rascal, you won.

items.el: Α: Δεν σκίζω και τα αρχίδια μου, είκοσι ευρώ κέρδισα όλα κι όλα.
items.en: A: I'm hardly rolling in it, I won twenty euros, that's all.

items.el: Β: Είκοσι ευρώ είναι τέσσερις μπίρες. Πάμε, μη μαλακίζεσαι.
items.en: B: Twenty euros is four beers. Come on, stop messing about.

blocks.title: Διάλογος 2: Στο γραφείο και στο σπίτι, δύο εκδοχές

items.el: (Στο γραφείο, με τη διευθύντρια)
items.en: (At the office, with the manager)

items.el: Α: Να πάρει η ευχή, κόλλησε πάλι ο εκτυπωτής.
items.en: A: Oh blast, the printer's jammed again.

items.el: Διευθύντρια: Τι στο καλό έχει πάθει σήμερα; Πάρε τον τεχνικό.
items.en: Manager: What on earth is wrong with it today? Call the technician.

items.el: Α: Αμέσως. Συγγνώμη, η καθυστέρηση είναι δική μου.
items.en: A: Right away. Sorry, the delay is my fault.

items.el: (Δέκα λεπτά μετά, στην κουζίνα του γραφείου, με τον συνάδελφο Νίκο)
items.en: (Ten minutes later, in the office kitchen, with colleague Nikos)

items.el: Α: Ρε Νίκο, αυτός ο κωλοεκτυπωτής θα με τρελάνει.
items.en: A: Nikos, this bloody printer is going to drive me mad.

items.el: Νίκος: Χέσ' τον. Στείλ' το στον τρίτο, εκεί δουλεύει.
items.en: Nikos: Forget it. Send it to the third floor, that one works.

items.el: Α: Και η αναφορά θέλει να είναι έτοιμη στις δύο. Γαμήθηκα.
items.en: A: And the report has to be ready by two. I'm screwed.

items.el: Νίκος: Μη μου λες μαλακίες, θα την τελειώσεις σε μία ώρα.
items.en: Nikos: Don't talk crap, you'll finish it in an hour.

items.el: (Το βράδυ, στο σπίτι, με τη γιαγιά)
items.en: (In the evening, at home, with grandma)

items.el: Γιαγιά: Πώς πήγε η δουλειά, παιδάκι μου;
items.en: Grandma: How was work, dear?

items.el: Α: Χάλια, γιαγιά. Ένα μπουρδέλο... συγγνώμη, ένα χάος!
items.en: A: Awful, Grandma. A total brothel... sorry, a total chaos!

items.el: Γιαγιά: Μπα σε καλό σου! Τι λόγια είναι αυτά; Έλα να φας.
items.en: Grandma: Goodness! What kind of language is that? Come and eat.

items.el: Α: Παναγία μου, πεινάω σαν λύκος.
items.en: A: Good Lord, I'm starving.

items.el: Γιαγιά: Τρώγε, και άσε τα βρομόλογα για τους φίλους σου.
items.en: Grandma: Eat, and save the dirty words for your friends.

blocks.title: Διάλογος 3: Όταν το αστείο γίνεται σοβαρό

items.el: Α: Έλα, ρε μαλάκα, πάλι άργησες μισή ώρα!
items.en: A: Come on, mate, you're half an hour late again!

items.el: Β: Χαχα, ξέρεις, η κίνηση...
items.en: B: Haha, you know, the traffic...

items.el: Α: Η κίνηση στ' αρχίδια μου. Κάθε φορά τα ίδια.
items.en: A: Traffic my arse. Same thing every time.

items.el: Β: Εντάξει, ρε, χαλάρωσε. Μαλακία μου.
items.en: B: OK, chill. My bad.

items.el: Α: Όχι, δεν χαλαρώνω. Είσαι μαλάκας, το ξέρεις;
items.en: A: No, I won't chill. You're an arsehole, you know that?

items.el: Β: Ε, όχι και μαλάκας. Το παράκανες τώρα.
items.en: B: Hey, not 'arsehole'. Now you've gone too far.

items.el: Α: Σε περίμενα σαν ηλίθιος στο κρύο.
items.en: A: I waited for you like an idiot in the cold.

items.el: Β: Έχεις δίκιο. Συγγνώμη, ειλικρινά. Κερνάω εγώ απόψε.
items.en: B: You're right. Sorry, honestly. Drinks are on me tonight.

items.el: Α: ...Καλά. Αλλά δύο γύρους.
items.en: A: ...Fine. But two rounds.

items.el: Β: Δύο γύρους, κερατά. Πάμε.
items.en: B: Two rounds, you old devil. Let's go.

blocks.title: Πώς διαβάζεις τη θερμοκρασία
items: **Who is the target?** A situation (*γαμώτο, σκατά, να πάρει*) is light; a person (*είσαι μαλάκας*) is heavier; a person's family or sacred things (*τη μάνα σου, την Παναγία σου*) is the heaviest.
**μου vs σου.** *Γαμώ το κέρατό μου* curses my own life; *γαμώ το κέρατό σου* attacks you. One pronoun turns a sigh into a provocation.
**ρε + smile = friendly; ρε + pause = hostile.** *Ρε μαλάκα* with a grin is a greeting; *Ρε... μαλάκα* with a pause and a stare is a challenge.
**Laughter is the safety catch.** Strong words exchanged while both people laugh are banter; the moment one person stops laughing, the same words are insults.
**Escalation is fast and de-escalation is explicit.** Greeks often say *Το παράκανες*, *Όχι και ...*, *Πλάκα κάνω* to reset the level; use them too.
**Mirror and stay one below.** As a learner, never go above the strongest level the other person has used with you.

blocks.title: Ένα μήνυμα φωνητικό: η Ελένη στην κολλητή της
blocks.text:
Μαρία, μαλάκα μου, πού είσαι; Σε παίρνω τρίτη φορά. Άκου τι έπαθα σήμερα, θα πεθάνεις.

Πάω το πρωί στη δουλειά, ε, και η κωλοδουλειά δεν φτάνει που με πληρώνει ψίχουλα, μου λέει ο Σταύρος, το αφεντικό, ότι πρέπει να μείνω μέχρι τις εννιά. Μέχρι τις εννιά, ρε! Εγώ, που είχα κλείσει θέατρο. Του λέω, ευγενικά, «Δυστυχώς έχω υποχρέωση», και μου κάνει μια φάτσα... Μέσα μου έλεγα «άντε γαμήσου», αλλά από έξω χαμογελούσα σαν μαλάκας. Έτσι κάνουμε όλοι, ε;

Τέλος πάντων, έμεινα μέχρι τις οχτώ. Βγαίνω, και τι να δω; Το λεωφορείο φεύγει μπροστά στα μάτια μου. Γαμώ την τύχη μου, σου λέω! Παίρνω ταξί. Ο ταξιτζής, ένας κερατάς με μουστάκι, έβριζε όλη την ώρα τους άλλους οδηγούς: «Πού πας, ρε μαλάκα; Τι κάνεις εκεί, ρε κωλόπαιδο;». Και μετά με κοιτάει στον καθρέφτη και μου λέει «Συγγνώμη, κοπέλα μου, για τα μπινελίκια». Πέθανα στο γέλιο!

Φτάνω στο θέατρο, και η παράσταση είχε ήδη αρχίσει. Δε γαμιέται, λέω, θα μπω στο διάλειμμα. Και ξέρεις ποιον βλέπω στο φουαγιέ; Τον Σταύρο! Με τη γυναίκα του! Αυτός που μου έλεγε ότι η δουλειά είναι επείγουσα. Μαλάκα, έμεινα κόκαλο. Με βλέπει, κοκκινίζει, και μου λέει «Α, τι σύμπτωση!». Τι σύμπτωση, παπάρια! Ήθελα να του πω «χέσε μας, ρε», αλλά η μάνα μου με μεγάλωσε καλά και είπα μόνο «Πράγματι».

Η παράσταση πάντως ήταν γαμάτη. Ο πρωταγωνιστής, αρχιδάτος τύπος, έπαιζε δύο ρόλους. Αλλά εγώ όλη την ώρα σκεφτόμουν αύριο στο γραφείο. Τι να κάνω; Να του πω κάτι; Ή να το χέσω και να κάνω ότι δεν έγινε τίποτα; Γιατί, αν μιλήσω, θα γίνει της πουτάνας.

Πάρε με όταν το ακούσεις, μαλάκα. Και μην πεις τίποτα στη μάνα σου, ξέρεις τι κουτσομπόλα είναι. Φιλιά! Α, και να πάρει η ευχή, ξέχασα πάλι να σου επιστρέψω το βιβλίο. Αύριο, ορκίζομαι!
blocks.en:
Maria, oh man, where are you? This is the third time I'm calling. Listen to what happened to me today, you'll die.

I go to work in the morning, right, and it's not enough that this crappy job pays me peanuts, Stavros, the boss, tells me I have to stay until nine. Until nine, man! Me, who had booked the theatre. I tell him, politely, 'Unfortunately I have a commitment', and he pulls a face... Inside I was thinking 'fuck off', but on the outside I was smiling like an idiot. That's what we all do, right?

Anyway, I stayed until eight. I come out, and what do I see? The bus leaves right in front of my eyes. Just my fucking luck, I'm telling you! I take a taxi. The taxi driver, some bastard with a moustache, was swearing at the other drivers the whole time: 'Where are you going, you wanker? What are you doing there, you little shit?'. And then he looks at me in the mirror and says, 'Sorry, miss, for the foul language.' I died laughing!

I get to the theatre, and the show had already started. Never mind, I say, I'll go in at the interval. And do you know who I see in the foyer? Stavros! With his wife! The man who told me the work was urgent. Dude, I froze. He sees me, goes red, and says 'Oh, what a coincidence!'. Coincidence my arse! I wanted to say 'give us a break, man', but my mother raised me well and I only said 'Indeed'.

The show was fucking great, though. The lead actor, a gutsy guy, played two roles. But the whole time I was thinking about tomorrow at the office. What do I do? Say something to him? Or forget about it and act like nothing happened? Because if I speak up, all hell will break loose.

Call me when you get this, babe. And don't say anything to your mum, you know what a gossip she is. Kisses! Oh, and damn it, I forgot to give you your book back again. Tomorrow, I swear!
